creative.body:
He reaches across the bed. I flinch before I think.

We both pretend it didn't happen. Then we go to sleep facing opposite walls.

That has been the last 11 months of my marriage.

I have been with my husband for 31 years. In May of last year I started letrozole. A small white pill, taken every morning with my coffee. The deal my oncologist made with me at my final radiation appointment.

5 years on this medication and a recurrence risk so low that we would, in her exact words, "take a quality-of-life approach to anything else that comes up."

What came up was the marriage.

Nobody at the oncology clinic told me the medication was going to do this to my body. They told me about hot flashes. They told me about joint stiffness. The leaflet had a paragraph about "vaginal symptoms" buried on the third page in language so soft I read it twice and still did not understand what it was saying.

What it was saying was that the medication would take from me, very slowly and very thoroughly, the part of my body that knew how to be touched.

The first time my husband reached for me and I felt a sharp, acid burn rather than warmth, I assumed it was a fluke. The fifth time I started crying afterward and could not explain why. The tenth time, I started flinching before he even touched me, because my body had learned what was coming and was trying to protect itself.

He stopped reaching first. Or maybe I stopped responding first. I cannot remember the order anymore.

What I remember is the night I lay in bed listening to him breathe and realized we had not touched each other in 7 weeks. Not sex. Just touch.

He had stopped putting his hand on the small of my back when he walked past me in the kitchen. I had stopped resting my feet on his under the dinner table. The whole vocabulary of small touch that 30 years of marriage builds had quietly, gently, stopped.

He was being careful. I was being careful. 2 careful people sleeping in the same bed and slowly losing each other.

I want to stop here and say something to whoever is reading this with the same knot in her chest I had for almost a year.

The standoff is not your fault. It is not his fault. It is not the marriage's fault.

The medication takes away the body's ability to be touched without pain. The marriage adapts the only way it knows how. By becoming careful. That is not a character flaw. That is physiology meeting 30 years of habit.

He did not stop wanting you. He stopped reaching, because the last 40 times he reached, your body told him no before your mouth could. He was not absent. He was being polite to a wound he did not know how to name.

The wanting was still there. The reaching had been trained out of him by the flinch. That is not the same thing.

Once I understood that, I understood the shape of the problem. The standoff was not emotional. It was mechanical. My body had stopped being a body that could be touched, and the rest of the marriage had reorganized itself around that fact in the quietest way possible.

I went to my oncologist's PA at the 6-month follow-up and tried to talk about it. She gave me the speech I now know every woman on an aromatase inhibitor gets.

Try Replens. Try coconut oil. Try a lubricant.

The conversation lasted about 3 minutes.

I tried Replens. I tried coconut oil. None of them did what they were supposed to do, because none of them was actually targeting the problem. They were addressing the surface. The problem was the tissue itself.

I went back to the same PA at the next visit and said the products had not worked. She gave me the same speech a second time, with the same kind voice.

Try Replens with more consistency. Try coconut oil before bed. Try a different lubricant.

I drove home from that appointment and pulled into my driveway and sat in the car with the engine off for 10 minutes and cried. I did not go to the drugstore. I did not pick up another tube of anything.

I sat there until I could breathe right, and I made a decision in that car that I would figure this out myself before the next appointment.

The PA was not going to be the one who solved it. Whatever was going to fix this was not on the shelf at CVS. I had been on that shelf for 8 months.

A woman whose name I do not know wrote a sentence on a survivor forum I will remember the rest of my life.

"Lube does nothing for the needle pain."

That was the moment I understood that what I had been handed at the oncology clinic was not the standard of care. It was the polite version of nothing.

The actual guideline, the one published by the American Society of Clinical Oncology in 2018, recommends a non-hormonal vaginal moisturizer used regularly as the first-line therapy.

A moisturizer. Not a lubricant. A product that rebuilds the tissue, not one that coats the surface for the next 20 minutes.

Replens hydrates the surface. Coconut oil sits on top. Lubricant covers the next 20 minutes. None of them rebuild the tissue. None of them restore the bacteria. None of them feed the colony. None of them sustain the work between doses.

The polite version of the standard does one of 4. The actual standard does 4 of 4. Once I saw that, I could not unsee it.

Somewhere in those weeks I asked a friend who had had a hysterectomy 2 years before me whether anyone had actually helped her. She gave me the name of a pelvic floor physical therapist she had seen.

I went. Her office smelled like clean laundry. She is a licensed PT, board-certified in pelvic health, the real credential. We talked for almost an hour before she touched me.

She told me she sees 5 to 6 women a week with iatrogenic dryness from aromatase inhibitors. The same standoff at home. The same drugstore products. She said the husbands are the ones who eventually call the office, not the women. The women come in apologizing for taking up the appointment slot.

She was the first clinician in 11 months who looked at me and said, in plain English, that what was happening to me was happening to a lot of women, and that the products my oncology office had given me were not designed to fix it.

There is one number she mentioned that I went home and looked up to verify.

Hyaluronic acid for vaginal atrophy in survivors has Class I evidence, the highest grade the literature awards, by a factor of 3 over its closest non-hormonal alternative.

I read that sentence sitting at my kitchen counter and said it out loud to nobody. The molecule with the strongest evidence in the literature was not the one in the tube the PA had given me.

That is when I found a small company called Avelle.

Avelle is a vaginal suppository, not a cream, used a few times a week. The hyaluronic acid hydrates the deep tissue the way the surface coatings cannot. The lactobacillus lactis helps rebalance the healthy bacterial environment that estrogen used to maintain on its own. The glycogen feeds those bacteria, replacing the substrate the medication had taken away. The polydextrose is a prebiotic fiber that keeps the colony working between applications.

Hydrate. Balance. Feed. Sustain. 4 layers, doing 4 different jobs, in a single suppository the size of a pencil eraser.

No estrogen. No phytoestrogens. No DHEA. No hormone analogs. No parabens. No phthalates. That ingredient list mattered to me more than I can explain.

I had spent 2 years being warned away from sea buckthorn oil, away from anything described as "plant-based estrogen support," away from products marketed for general menopause that had been quietly retrofitted with botanicals my oncologist would not approve.

"Natural" is not the same as "safe for an aromatase inhibitor patient." I needed a molecule list I could verify, not a vibe.

Hyaluronic acid is a sugar-based molecule the body already makes. It is not a hormone. It does not bind estrogen receptors. Lactobacillus lactis is a bacterium. Glycogen is a sugar. Polydextrose is a fiber. There are 0 ingredients in the formulation that an aromatase inhibitor patient is told to avoid.

I printed the Avelle handout for my oncologist. I brought it to my next appointment along with the ASCO guideline. She read both, looked at me, and said she had no objection.

That sentence. No objection. I had been waiting for some version of that sentence for almost a year.

The first month, I noticed I was less afraid of bedtime. The dryness had eased enough that I could imagine, for the first time in almost a year, that touch might not hurt.

The second month, I started reaching for him again. My hand on his back when he was at the sink. My foot on his under the dinner table.

The third month, we made love for the first time in 14 months.

The fourth month, I realized I was not flinching anymore. He could reach across the bed and I would meet his hand. The standoff was over.

There is a version of this letter where I tell you to think about it. To do your research. I am not going to write that version, because I lived in that version for 11 months and it cost me almost a year of my marriage.

There are 2 paths from where you are sitting tonight.

The first path is the one you are already on. You can keep 2 careful people sleeping in the same bed and slowly losing each other. You can keep waiting for your body to come back on its own. It will not.

The medication is doing exactly what it was prescribed to do, which is to suppress the estrogen that used to keep your tissue alive. There is no version of this where the carefulness resolves itself.

The second path is to interrupt the careful.

Bring the handout to your oncologist. Hear the no-objection language for yourself. Try the actual first-line standard for 90 days and find out whether your body responds the way mine did.

The wasted thing is not the box on the bathroom counter. The wasted thing is the next 9 months of your marriage spent the way the last 9 months were spent.

There is no third path. The careful does not resolve itself. The careful only gets quieter, and then quieter, until you are 2 roommates who used to be married.

When I went to the order page, I saw a 90-day money-back guarantee printed right there. I sat with that for a long minute. I had sat in oncology waiting rooms for almost a year by that point, and I had never once heard a drug rep, or a manufacturer, or a pharmacy, or anyone in the building, offer to give a patient her money back if the prescription did not work.

The Replens did not come with a refund offer. The coconut oil did not. The lubricant the PA had recommended did not.

The first time, in the entire 11 months of the standoff, that anyone had said in writing that if their product did not do the work they would give me my money back, was a small company I had found on a survivor forum at one in the morning. That alone changed how I felt about clicking the button.

I had read enough by then to understand why they made the batches small. The lactobacillus lactis is a live culture, and the glycogen it feeds on has a finite shelf-active window once the suppository is formed. They batch-produce because they will not ship a bottle whose colony has aged out of viability sitting in a warehouse.

The trade-off is that they sell out for a few weeks at a time. If they are in stock the night you read this, that is the night to order. You do not wait until next week.

If your husband still reaches for you, even occasionally, even hesitantly, even after months of being met with a flinch, you have the only thing this product cannot give you. He has not given up. The wanting is still there.

The standoff does not end on its own. It ends when one of you breaks the careful, and tonight that one is you.
creative.title: He Did Not Stop Wanting You. He Stopped Reaching.
